title: How businesses exchange orders and invoices electronically (EDI)
audience: A curious adult from a different field, with no assumed knowledge of supply chains or business software.
scope: Covers electronic data interchange (EDI) and e-invoicing between suppliers, retailers and wholesalers, with examples from the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Leaves out consumer e-commerce checkout, payments and customs.
learningGoals: Explain why companies exchange business documents as structured data instead of e-mail and PDF.
Describe the order, despatch advice and invoice cycle between a supplier and a retailer.
Explain what an EDI service provider and its network do.
Name the main difficulties: partner-specific formats, data quality, compliance deadlines and trust.

introduction.whatItIs: Electronic data interchange (EDI) is the automatic exchange of business documents, such as orders, delivery notes and invoices, between the computer systems of two companies, in an agreed machine-readable format. Nobody retypes anything: the order leaves the retailer's system and lands in the supplier's system.
introduction.whyItMatters: A supermarket chain may receive deliveries from hundreds of suppliers every day. If every order and invoice were an e-mail with a PDF, people would spend their days copying numbers, and every typo would turn into a wrong delivery or a disputed invoice. Structured exchange makes the chain faster, cheaper and more reliable, and many retailers now require it.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of a universal travel adapter. Each country has its own socket; the adapter lets your charger work everywhere. An EDI provider is the adapter between a supplier's system and each retailer's system.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: A plug adapter only fits shapes. EDI also has to agree on meaning: which product code, which delivery address, which price, and what to do when a delivery is short. That shared meaning, and checking it, is most of the work.

participants.name: Supplier
participants.role: Makes or wholesales goods and delivers them to retailers.
participants.caresAbout: Getting every order right, deliveries accepted, and invoices paid without extra admin.

participants.name: Retailer or buying organisation
participants.role: Orders from many suppliers and receives goods at distribution centres.
participants.caresAbout: Shelves stocked, deliveries announced in advance, invoices that match what arrived.

participants.name: EDI service provider
participants.role: Runs the network that translates, checks and delivers messages between companies (Transus is one).
participants.caresAbout: Reliable delivery, fast onboarding of new partners and keeping customers for years.

participants.name: ERP partner or IT team
participants.role: Connects the company's business software (ERP) to the provider.
participants.caresAbout: Integrations that keep working without constant attention.

participants.name: Tax authority or regulator
participants.role: Sets rules such as mandatory e-invoicing and security requirements.
participants.caresAbout: Correct, verifiable invoices and resilient supply chains.

participants.name: Logistics provider
participants.role: Transports and receives goods on behalf of the retailer.
participants.caresAbout: Knowing what is on each pallet before it arrives.

concepts.meaning: A published structure that says where each piece of information goes in an electronic document. EDIFACT is an older international standard widely used in retail; UBL is an XML-based standard common in e-invoicing.
concepts.example: An EDIFACT order message is called ORDERS; the invoice is INVOIC.
concepts.whyItMatters: Without a shared structure, a receiving system cannot read the document automatically.

media.title: Message standard (EDIFACT, UBL)
media.alt: Message standard (EDIFACT, UBL): An EDIFACT order message is called ORDERS; the invoice is INVOIC.
media.caption: Without a shared structure, a receiving system cannot read the document automatically.

concepts.meaning: One company's specific rules within a standard: which optional fields it requires, which codes it uses.
concepts.example: Two supermarkets both use EDIFACT orders, but one requires a delivery-window field and the other does not.
concepts.whyItMatters: This is why "we support EDIFACT" is not enough; each partner must be mapped individually.

media.alt: Implementation guideline: Two supermarkets both use EDIFACT orders, but one requires a delivery-window field and the other does not.
media.caption: This is why "we support EDIFACT" is not enough; each partner must be mapped individually.

concepts.meaning: The set of rules that converts a company's own data format into the partner's format and back.
concepts.example: The supplier's ERP exports a CSV file; the mapping turns it into the retailer's EDIFACT invoice.
concepts.whyItMatters: Mapping is the main cost of adding a partner; tools like AI-assisted mapping aim to shrink it.

media.title: Mapping
media.alt: Mapping: The supplier's ERP exports a CSV file; the mapping turns it into the retailer's EDIFACT invoice.
media.caption: Mapping is the main cost of adding a partner; tools like AI-assisted mapping aim to shrink it.

concepts.meaning: A despatch advice is an electronic message announcing what is in a delivery. An SSCC (serial shipping container code) is a unique GS1 number printed as a barcode on each pallet label.
concepts.example: Before the truck arrives, the retailer's DC receives a DESADV listing pallet SSCCs; at the dock it scans each label and knows the contents.
concepts.whyItMatters: Unannounced or wrongly labelled pallets can be refused or slow down the warehouse.

media.caption: Unannounced or wrongly labelled pallets can be refused or slow down the warehouse.

concepts.meaning: Automatic checks that a message is complete and follows the rules before it is delivered.
concepts.example: An invoice missing the buyer's identification number is blocked and the sender gets an alert.
concepts.whyItMatters: Catching errors early is cheaper than a rejected invoice weeks later.

media.title: Validation
media.alt: Validation: An invoice missing the buyer's identification number is blocked and the sender gets an alert.
media.caption: Catching errors early is cheaper than a rejected invoice weeks later.

concepts.meaning: An e-invoice is a structured invoice a system can read, not a PDF. Peppol is a European network for delivering such documents between registered participants.
concepts.example: From 2027 many German companies must send invoices as XRechnung or ZUGFeRD files or via Peppol.
concepts.whyItMatters: Governments are making structured invoices mandatory, which drives many companies to EDI providers.

media.caption: Governments are making structured invoices mandatory, which drives many companies to EDI providers.

concepts.meaning: A provider's set of already-connected companies. If your customer is already on the network, connecting is mostly configuration.
concepts.example: Transus states more than 100,000 trading partners are reachable through its network.
concepts.whyItMatters: Networks create value for everyone on them; this is why providers compete on reach.

historyNote: A few turning points that explain current practice, mainly from a European perspective.

history.change: Large companies began exchanging documents electronically using industry-specific formats, which led to international standardisation, including the UN/EDIFACT standard.
history.whyItMatters: Common standards made it possible to connect many partners instead of building bespoke links for each.

history.change: Value-added networks and EDI service providers offered connections as a service, and web EDI portals let small suppliers without IT staff take part.
history.whyItMatters: EDI spread from large corporations to small suppliers, often because retailers required it.

history.change: Retailers increasingly made EDI, despatch advice and SSCC labels mandatory for suppliers; cloud platforms replaced in-house converters.
history.whyItMatters: EDI became a condition for doing business with major chains, not an optional efficiency.

history.change: Governments began mandating structured e-invoicing between businesses (for example Germany from 2025 for receiving and 2027-2028 for sending), and security laws such as NIS2 raised expectations of suppliers.
history.whyItMatters: Compliance deadlines now drive adoption alongside retailer demands.

walkthrough.title: A pallet of frozen fish from order to payment (fictional example)
walkthrough.setup: Marieke runs the order desk at a fictional seafood producer that supplies a supermarket chain. Her company uses an EDI provider; the supermarket uses its own ordering system. Names and numbers are illustrative.

steps.title: The supermarket orders
steps.whatHappens: At night the supermarket's system creates an order for 40 boxes of frozen cod and sends it as an EDIFACT ORDERS message to the provider.
steps.whyItMatters: Nobody at the supermarket types or e-mails anything.

steps.title: The provider translates and checks
steps.whatHappens: The provider converts the order into the format Marieke's ERP understands and checks that article codes and delivery location are present.
steps.whyItMatters: Marieke's system never needs to know the supermarket's specific format.
steps.watchOut: If an article code is unknown, the message is blocked and Marieke gets an alert explaining the problem.

steps.title: Marieke confirms
steps.whatHappens: Her ERP shows the order; she confirms 36 boxes because stock is short, and an order response goes back automatically.
steps.whyItMatters: The supermarket learns about the shortfall before the truck arrives, not at the dock.

steps.title: Pallets are labelled and announced
steps.whatHappens: The warehouse packs two pallets, prints SSCC labels, and a despatch advice listing both pallets and their best-before dates is sent.
steps.whyItMatters: The distribution centre can plan the receipt and scan the pallets quickly.

steps.title: The invoice follows
steps.whatHappens: After delivery the ERP creates an invoice for 36 boxes; the provider converts it into the supermarket's invoice format and delivers it.
steps.whyItMatters: Because the invoice matches the order response and despatch advice, it can be approved automatically.
steps.watchOut: If the price in the invoice differs from the supermarket's price list, the invoice may be rejected and paid late.

walkthrough.outcome: The fish arrives announced, the invoice matches, and payment follows on time. Marieke spent minutes on an exception instead of hours retyping documents.

valueAndIncentives.title: Who benefits
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Suppliers save manual work and avoid fines; retailers get predictable deliveries and invoices that match automatically.
valueAndIncentives.example: A supplier with 30 retail customers would otherwise follow 30 different invoice rules by hand.

valueAndIncentives.title: Who pays
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Usually the supplier pays the provider a subscription; some providers, including Transus, use a fixed monthly price with unlimited messages and partners.
valueAndIncentives.example: Transus lists plans from EUR 79 per month for web EDI to a Premium plan on request.

valueAndIncentives.title: Why retailers push
valueAndIncentives.explanation: The retailer gets most of the efficiency but the supplier bears most of the setup, so retailers use listing conditions to drive adoption.
valueAndIncentives.example: A DIY chain requires EDI and SSCC labels from every supplier.

challenges.title: Every partner is a little different
challenges.whyHard: Standards allow options, so each retailer has its own guideline that also changes over time.
challenges.tradeOff: Flexibility for large retailers versus mapping work for every supplier.
challenges.example: Two chains use the same EDIFACT order but require different fields.
challenges.commonApproach: Providers maintain libraries of retailer requirements and increasingly use AI to propose mappings; specialists still review unusual cases.

challenges.title: Data quality at the source
challenges.whyHard: A perfectly delivered message with a wrong price or product code still causes a dispute.
challenges.tradeOff: Strict validation blocks errors but can also block urgent orders.
challenges.example: An invoice is rejected because the price list was updated after the order.
challenges.commonApproach: Validation with clear alerts and monitoring; it cannot fix bad master data in the ERP.

challenges.title: Compliance deadlines
challenges.whyHard: E-invoicing rules differ per country and arrive on fixed dates.
challenges.tradeOff: Building per-country solutions versus one flexible platform.
challenges.commonApproach: Providers add new formats as configuration and partner with specialists for networks like Peppol.

challenges.title: Trust and continuity
challenges.whyHard: If the provider fails, orders stop across thousands of relationships.
challenges.tradeOff: Outsourcing reduces in-house effort but concentrates risk.
challenges.example: Customers under NIS2 audit their EDI provider's security.
challenges.commonApproach: Certified security management, encrypted transport, backup data centres and incident procedures.

misconceptions.belief: EDI is just sending files by e-mail.
misconceptions.reality: EDI is structured data that systems process automatically, with agreed formats, validation and delivery confirmation.

misconceptions.belief: You need a large IT department to do EDI.
misconceptions.reality: Small suppliers can use web portals or let a provider and an ERP partner handle the integration.

misconceptions.belief: A PDF invoice is an e-invoice.
misconceptions.reality: Under the new mandates an e-invoice must be a structured file such as XRechnung or a Peppol document.

takeaways: EDI replaces retyping with structured data that systems exchange directly.
The hard part is shared meaning: each partner's rules, mapping and data quality.
Providers create value through their network, their library of partner requirements and their exception handling.
Retailer demands and government e-invoicing mandates are the main reasons companies start.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why can't a supplier simply say "we support EDIFACT" and be connected to every retailer?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because each retailer uses its own implementation guideline within the standard.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The standard allows options; each partner needs a mapping that matches its specific required fields and codes.

knowledgeChecks.question: In the walkthrough, why did the invoice get approved automatically?
knowledgeChecks.answer: It matched the order response and despatch advice.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The supermarket could compare the invoiced 36 boxes with what was confirmed and announced.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why would a retailer care whether its supplier's EDI provider is secure?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because a failure or breach at the provider can stop or corrupt its supply chain.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Under NIS2 essential entities must manage supply-chain risk, including their suppliers' providers.
